ledger.claim: Left-digit effect: $2.99 is perceived as closer to $2 than $3; nine-ending effect appears when the leftmost digit changes
ledger.source: Thomas, M. & Morwitz, V. (2005) Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition. Journal of Consumer Research 32(1), 54-64
ledger.caveats: Experiments used student participants and pens; summary page gives no percentage effect sizes. $3.29 vs $3.30 in script is our illustration.

ledger.claim: $9 price endings increased demand in all three field experiments, more for new items than items sold in earlier years; may work better with limited information
ledger.source: Anderson, E. & Simester, D. (2003) Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments. Quantitative Marketing and Economics 1(1), 93-110
ledger.confidence: high for demand result; medium for mechanism
ledger.caveats: Abstract gives no percentage lift. Do not use the $34 to $39 example.

ledger.claim: Used-car prices drop at each 10,000-mile threshold ($150 to $200); cars at 79,900-79,999 miles sold ~$210 above 80,000-80,100 but only $10 below 79,800-79,899; >22 million wholesale transactions
ledger.source: Lacetera, N., Pope, D. & Sydnor, J. Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market. NBER Working Paper 17030 (digest: NBER Digest, Sept 2011)
ledger.caveats: Check whether a later journal version changes figures. Authors attribute inattention mainly to final buyers.

ledger.claim: Shoppers behaved as if a 1 cent gap were 15-25 cents; firms priced as if 1.5-3 cents; 1,710 products in 248 stores; one-quarter to one-third of prices ended in 99 cents
ledger.source: Strulov-Shlain, A. (2023) More than a Penny's Worth: Left-Digit Bias and Firm Pricing. Review of Economic Studies 90(5), 2612-2645 (figures read from Chicago Booth Review, 18 Feb 2020, on the 2019 working paper)
ledger.type: secondary summary of working paper; published version exists
ledger.caveats: VERIFY all numbers against the published Review of Economic Studies paper before final render. Data come from one US retailer and a set of chains.

ledger.claim: Cash-register origin of 99 endings is a legend; no documentation found
ledger.source: Fordham news story on R. Schindler keynote (call it legend); CBC Under the Influence (unsourced)
ledger.caveats: Presented as legend only. 1875 and 1880 origin claims are unverified and not used.

ledger.claim: Consumers judge the difference between $4.00 and $2.99 as larger than between $4.01 and $3.00, though the numeric differences are identical (left-digit bias); stronger when prices are seen side by side
ledger.source: Sokolova, T., Seenivasan, S. & Thomas, M. (2020) The Left-Digit Bias: When and Why Are Consumers Penny Wise and Pound Foolish? Journal of Marketing Research 57(4)
ledger.type: primary (open-access abstract, shown on screen as a screenshot)
ledger.caveats: Used on screen while the voiceover names the left-digit effect; the screenshot highlights the abstract's own wording.

ledger.claim: On-screen imagery: US $100 note photo, journal screenshots, generic cars and shoppers
ledger.source: Screenshots supplied by the channel owner; $100 note photo supplied by the channel owner (check its licence before publishing); cars, shoppers, shelves and storefront are original flat illustrations with no real brand marks
ledger.caveats: Field-experiment and cashier scenes are illustrations of the cited findings, captioned as such.
